c.tagline: A Caribbean island escape of turquoise 'sea of seven colors' waters and Raizal island culture

card: Widely accepted at hotels and larger restaurants; cash useful for beach vendors and small shops

taxi.fare: Fixed zone-based fares rather than metered
taxi.fareNote: San Andrés taxis charge set rates by zone; confirm the fare before departure

emergency.note: 123 connects to police, fire, and medical services across Colombia

religion: Christianity (Roman Catholic majority, strong Protestant/Baptist presence tied to Raizal heritage)
walk: The town center (El Centro) is walkable, but San Luis, West View, and La Loma require a golf cart, moto-taxi, or car to reach

safety.safety: Generally safe and tourism-oriented; standard beach-destination precautions apply
safety.crime: Petty theft on crowded beaches is the main concern

hood_landmark.La Loma: La Loma's hilltop First Baptist Church

avoid.reason: Stay out of the inland residential barrios away from the tourist strip after dark, where occasional gang-related crime occurs.
Watch belongings on busy Spratt Bight beach, decline street drug offers firmly, and agree rental and water-sport prices in advance.

hood_desc: The compact commercial hub with shops, restaurants, and the main hotel strip; the natural base for most visitors.
A quieter stretch of beach on the island's east side, popular with locals and travelers wanting fewer crowds.
A hilltop Raizal community with island views and a historic Baptist church, offering a glimpse of local culture beyond the beach resorts.

water.note: Fresh water is scarce on the island; drink bottled water only.

transit.sys: Golf cart rentals, moto-taxis, and small buses circling the island's ring road
transit.pay: Cash fares for buses and moto-taxis; golf carts rented by the day
transit.map: Not centrally published; the island's single ring road makes navigation simple
transit.note: Renting a golf cart is the most popular way for visitors to get around the island

transport.air: Gustavo Rojas Pinilla International Airport (ADZ), about 10 min from town
transport.bus: Small local buses circle the island's ring road
transport.ferry: Catamaran ferry service to Providencia island
transport.car: Rental cars, scooters, and golf carts are available for the island's compact ring road

net.w: Free wifi standard in hotels and cafes
net.fwn: Free wifi widely available in hotels
net.ap: A Claro or Movistar tourist SIM or eSIM

tip.s: 10% is often added automatically ('propina voluntaria') at restaurants; check the bill
tip.r: 10% is customary if not already included

landmarks: Johnny Cay
A palm-fringed islet of white sand and reggae shacks floating in the 'sea of seven colours', reached by a short boat hop from town.
Hoyo Soplador
At the island's southern tip, a natural blowhole shoots seawater metres into the air whenever waves surge through its coral tunnels.
La Piscinita (West View)
A crystal-clear natural rock pool on the west coast where snorkellers slip in among swarms of rainbow-hued tropical fish.
Spratt Bight Beach
The island's liveliest beach fronts a pedestrian promenade with dazzling views across turquoise shallows to Johnny Cay offshore.
Acuario & Haynes Cay
Waist-deep sandbanks between two tiny cays create a natural aquarium where visitors wade among stingrays and shimmering fish shoals.
Cueva de Morgan (Morgan's Cave)
A coral cavern where pirate Henry Morgan allegedly stashed treasure, now paired with a small museum of island buccaneering lore.
Rocky Cay
Wade across a shallow sandbar to this mini islet beside a rusting shipwreck, one of the island's most photogenic swimming spots.
First Baptist Church (La Loma)
A gleaming white 1847 timber church on the island's highest hill, spiritual home of the Raizal community with sweeping sea views.
Big Pond (La Laguna)
A freshwater lagoon in the hilly interior where locals coax semi-tame caimans to the shore beneath mango and cotton trees.
Jardín Botánico de San Andrés
University-run gardens with a lookout tower rising above native trees, revealing the reef-ringed east coast in a panorama of blues.

train.note: San Andrés is a small Caribbean island 700 km from the Colombian mainland with no railway of any kind. Access is by air only - there are flights from Bogotá, Medellín, Cartagena and Panama City.

bus.note: No coach routes exist on an island. Local buses circle the 30 km ring road around San Andrés for a very low flat fare, and rented golf carts and mopeds are the usual way visitors get about. There is no terminal.

intl.op: Conocemos Navegando / Catamarán El Sensación — tickets at the San Andrés muelle or through local agents

ferry.note: There is no international ferry and no boat to mainland Colombia - the sea crossing is far too long, so everyone flies in. The Providencia catamaran is the one real sailing, taking about three hours in often rough open sea; it runs a few days a week, is frequently cancelled in bad weather, and many travellers prefer the short flight. Book ahead in the December-January and Easter peaks.

full.name: Providencia
full.blurb: A quieter sister island reached by catamaran or short flight, with Old Providence McBean Lagoon and Crab Cay's reef for snorkeling.
